amendments.because: Listing every test in the new fix's Done-when duplicates next's lines and grows without limit; the fix names the failed run instead
amendments.done_when: When the latest nightly full run failed, forge next names the platforms and failing tests and gives the forge fix start command for them

done_when: When the latest scheduled run of a workflow failed, forge next names its failed jobs and every failing test, and gives one forge fix start command for that failed run (or the started fix's next step)

findings.body:
Gain 2, Work 3, Harm 2
The parser at this line recognizes only pytest-style `FAILED` or `ERROR` lines containing `::`. A scheduled JavaScript or Go job can fail with named tests in its log while `forge next` lists only the job. The command-level proof supplies pytest output only. Forge's shipped guidance supports these runners, but this is an additional runner case outside the named proof.
findings.title: Follow-up: name JavaScript and Go test failures in scheduled runs

findings.body:
Gain 2, Work 2, Harm 2
The request reads only the newest 100 scheduled runs across workflows. A workflow scheduled every five minutes can fill that page in about eight hours, hiding another workflow's failed daily run. [GitHub permits five-minute schedules](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/workflow-syntax). The coordinator expressly narrowed this case to a follow-up.
findings.title: Follow-up: retain failed daily workflows beyond the recent-run page

stop.reason: Coordinator (Harm 2, reversible): back to one GitHub request — recent scheduled runs (per page 100), newest per workflow id — so next stays fast with many workflows; alerts key by workflow id. A very frequent schedule crowding out a daily run is a follow-up.

why: A failing nightly full run on macOS or Windows is easy to miss, and Windows stayed red for days unseen
